items.rationale: To keep every student, including those with no enrollment, the students table must be the preserved (left) side of a LEFT JOIN. An INNER JOIN drops unmatched students; a LEFT JOIN from enrollments keeps all enrollments, which adds no unenrolled students.
INNER JOIN returns only students with at least one matching enrollment, which is exactly the mailing list. A LEFT JOIN would also return students with no enrollments.

A LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched students with NULL enrollment columns, and filtering for enrollment_id IS NULL keeps only those students. An INNER JOIN has no unmatched rows, so options a and d cannot find the students; option b returns the enrolled students instead.

A LEFT JOIN returns one row per matching enrollment (3 + 1 + 2 = 6) plus one row with NULLs for the student with no enrollments (Cy), so 7. Answering 4 assumes one row per student (M3); 6 forgets that unmatched students are kept.
For a department with no courses, the LEFT JOIN produces one row with NULL course columns. COUNT(*) counts that row and gives 1; COUNT(courses.course_id) ignores NULLs and gives 0.

The unmatched student's row has NULL in enrollments.term, and NULL = 'Fall' is not true, so WHERE removes the row. The filter on the right-hand table effectively turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN; to keep them, put the condition in the ON clause.
